newsitem.title: USA: US Labor--experimental CPI to show lower inflation.
newsitem.headline: US Labor--experimental CPI to show lower inflation.

text.p: The Labor Department on Thursday, unveiling a new experimental consumer price index, said it now appears that it will show a lower growth rate for inflation of approximately one-quarter of one percent per year over the official CPI now in use.

In a briefing for reporters, John Greenlees, Assistant Commissioner for the department's Bureau of Labor Statistics, said that a partial adoption of the geometric mean formula used with the new experimental index could be expected to have a downward impact of between zero and one quarter of one percent per year, depending on how extensively it is used.
Labor said it expected to announce the findings of its research by the end of this year, including which CPI basic indexes are best calculated with the experimental formula.
It said the likely date for implementation of the new data would be with release of the January 1999 CPI data.
Greenlees told reporters that it was highly likely that something would be done at that time, although it was uncertain what changes would be made. That would be determined as the experiment went on.

Labor, which issued both an experimental CPI plus a test CPI that was more accurate for historical comparisons, said that over the period from December 1990 through February 1997 the experimental index rose 16.2 percent, compared with 18.6 percent for the test index.
The average rate of growth in the experimental index over the period was 2.46 percent, 0.34 percentage point lower than the 2.80 percent annual growth rate of the test series.
The department said that among the major items, the largest differences between the two indexes were in food and beverages, apparal and upkeep, medical care and entertainment.
Beginning April 22, the geometric means experimental index and the test arithmethic index will be released monthly one week after release of the official CPI.
